source.title: LLM-Safety Evaluations Lack Robustness
source.authors: Tim Beyer; Sophie Xhonneux; Simon Geisler; G. Gidel; Leo Schwinn; Stephan Gunnemann

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates suffix-based jailbreak attacks on safety-trained chat models, a different intervention from fine-tuning or measuring token-position KL, and reports attack success rates.
record.gate_note: The study tests GCG suffix attacks and reports their harmful-response success rates under different implementation settings. Its prefilling attack is included in a judge-comparison study, but the text does not report prefilling success rates, so it does not test that part of V4. The affirmative-target loss experiment in Appendix A.4 measures loss, not harmful compliance; the judge-disagreement results are recorded under fits_no_version. No results test fine-tuning-induced safety loss, token-position KL, safety localization in weights, causes of shallowness, or deepening interventions.
record.test_reason: The study runs GCG adversarial suffixes against safety-trained Llama chat models and reports harmful-response attack success rates. That bears on the suffix part of V4, even though the study's aim is to show that evaluation setup changes the measured ASR. Its prefilling attack appears only in the judge-disagreement comparison, as CAIS-minus-StrongREJECT differences, with no absolute success rate. No results address fine-tuning, per-token KL, weight localization, causes of shallowness or deepening.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors argue that LLM safety evaluations are unreliable because of small and inconsistently subsampled datasets, undocumented implementation details, unmatched attack budgets, biased optimization targets, greedy-only generation and biased automated judges. They recommend larger datasets, standardized and documented setups, budget-controlled comparisons, reporting overrefusal, multiple judges with human checks, and distributional sampling.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines GCG jailbreak success and robustness-evaluation methodology, not harmful or benign fine-tuning, token-position KL, or safety-deepening training.
record.method_sensitivity: GCG ASR varies with whitespace handling, chat template, token filtering, quantization, and presence of a system prompt; judge disagreement varies by attack and model.

fits_no_version.finding: The HarmBench Llama-2-13B and StrongREJECT Gemma-2B judges differ in ASR by up to 25% per attack and 24% per model, over 5.27M generations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Automated jailbreak judges disagree in attack- and model-specific ways, distorting ASR comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Safety-trained variants (circuit breakers, CAT, LLM-LAT) show very high loss on a 'Sure, here...' affirmative target even for a benign prompt (Appendix A.4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety training that targets fixed affirmative openings makes those openings improbable, which can inflate apparent robustness to target-based attacks.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the GCG attack-success results. Its large judge-comparison experiment did not compare the two classifiers with human ground truth, and it states that not all attack runs completed.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix A.3 Figure 5 shows attack-progress curves for implementation configurations also summarized by the final ASRs in Table 1; the separately plotted step-by-step values are figure-only and are not transcribed. Appendix A.4 reports affirmative-target loss rather than harmful-compliance behaviour. Appendix A.6's per-attack and per-model figure details are not reported as separate efficacy results; the text's aggregate judge-disagreement findings are recorded in r9-r10.

untested.parts: Prefilling success rates (prefilling appears only as a judge-difference bar in Figure 8), decoding changes, suffix attacks on non-Llama models, and single-trial or greedy-only success of suffixes.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Localization of safety in a small set of parameters.
Causes of shallowness. The paper only speculates that low dataset diversity contributes.

record.verdict_notes: This is a position paper. Its GCG experiments are methodological case studies, not a test of shallow alignment, so the V4 verdicts rest on incidental ASR figures without a no-attack baseline. The reader's third label wrongly linked judge-disagreement rows r9–r10 to V4; it is dropped. The paper mentions shallow alignment (Qi et al.) only as a speculated consequence of low dataset diversity.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
The study tests GCG suffix attacks, but does not report the efficacy of compliant-start prefilling or decoding changes.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether data or training objectives produce safety shallowness.
Training to deepen safety behaviour and whether it remains effective.

relationships.condition: GCG suffix attacks, many-trial, against Llama-2-7b-chat and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with correct implementations
relationships.reason: Suffix attacks reach 91% ASR on Llama-2 (r1) and 0.71–0.85 on Llama-3.1 across reasonable configurations (r3–r7). No no-suffix baseline is reported.
relationships.display_finding: Suffix attacks reached 91% ASR on Llama-2 and 0.71–0.85 on Llama-3.1 across reasonable configurations, with no no-suffix baseline reported.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: GCG suffix attacks, many-trial, against Llama-2-7b-chat and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with correct implementations
source_check.reason: r1 reports 91% many-trial ASR; r3–r7 report 0.71–0.85. These results support suffix bypass in the tested settings, without establishing an increase over a matched no-suffix baseline.

relationships.condition: Implementation choices: whitespace token handling, chat template, token filter, quantization, system prompt
relationships.reason: Measured suffix success swings from 0.47 to 0.91 with minor setup changes: 63% vs 91% for whitespace handling, 0.71–0.85 across template, filter and dtype, and 0.47 with no system prompt. The measured size of V4's effect therefore depends on these choices (r1–r8).
relationships.display_finding: Suffix success was 63% or 91% depending on whitespace handling, 0.71–0.85 across template, token filter and dtype, and 0.47 with no system prompt, so the measured effect depends on these choices.

source_check.condition: Implementation choices: whitespace token handling, chat template, token filter, quantization, system prompt
source_check.reason: r1–r2 show 91% versus 63% from whitespace handling; r3–r8 show configuration-dependent ASRs of 0.47–0.85 on Llama-3.1. This qualifies measured suffix effectiveness, rather than showing its absence.

relation.reason: The study reports its own harmful-response attack success rates for optimized suffixes against safety-trained models.

tranche.reason: Its own GCG implementation ablations measure harmful-response suffix success and its dependence on evaluation choices, bearing directly on V4 through a different experimental approach.

source_check.notes: The quoted scalar ASRs do not identify which of the two judges they use; no matched no-suffix ASRs or uncertainty intervals accompany these rows. Appendix A.6 includes direct and prefilling attacks but reports judge discrepancies rather than absolute bypass rates.

statements.correction: Llama-2-7b-chat-hf; first 100 HarmBench prompts; Meta template without system prompt; 250 GCG iterations; correct whitespace handling: 91% many-trial ASR; misaligned handling: 63%; no matched no-suffix baseline reported; supports V4 with implementation-dependent scope.
statements.problem: The 91% and 63% values are correct, but this study does not establish a challenge to V4: the misaligned implementation still achieves substantial suffix success. It demonstrates attack-implementation sensitivity.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GCG suffix attacks under the tested Llama chat-model configurations
reader_labels.reason: The reported many-trial ASRs show substantial attack success, including 91% with correctly handled whitespace and values from 0.71 to 0.85 in several Llama-3.1 configurations (r1, r3-r7).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Misaligned whitespace and absence of a system prompt
reader_labels.reason: Success is lower in these settings: 63% with misaligned whitespace and 0.47 without a system message (r2, r8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Implementation choices for GCG and judge setup
reader_labels.reason: The study reports substantial ASR differences across implementation configurations, while its large-scale judge comparison finds attack- and model-specific judge discrepancies; the latter is not itself a measurement of attack efficacy (r3-r10).
